:::{#thm-orthogonal-complement-subspace}
#### An orthogonal complement is a subspace

For any set $\mathcal{X}$ of vectors in $\reals^p$,
$\mathcal{X}^\perp$ (@def-orthogonal-complement)
is a subspace of $\reals^p$ (@def-subspace).

:::

::: proof

$\mathcal{X}^\perp$ is not empty:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vecf{x} \cdot \vzero &= \sum_i x_i \cd 0 \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

for every $\vecf{x}$,
so $\vzero \in \mathcal{X}^\perp$.
Let $\vecf{u}, \vecf{w} \in \mathcal{X}^\perp$, let $c \in \reals$,
and let $\vecf{x} \in \mathcal{X}$.

**Addition.**

$$
\ba
\vecf{x} \cdot (\vecf{u} + \vecf{w})
&= \vecf{x} \cdot \vecf{u} + \vecf{x} \cdot \vecf{w}
&& \text{(@thm-dot-linear, special case } a \text{ and } b \text{ both equal to } 1 \text{)}
\\
&= 0 + 0
&& \text{(} \vecf{u}, \vecf{w} \in \mathcal{X}^\perp \text{)}
\\
&= 0.
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\ea
$$

**Scalar multiplication.**

$$
\ba
\vecf{x} \cdot (c\,\vecf{u})
&= c\,(\vecf{x} \cdot \vecf{u})
&& \text{(@thm-dot-linear, special case } b = 0 \text{)}
\\
&= c \cd 0
&& \text{(} \vecf{u} \in \mathcal{X}^\perp \text{)}
\\
&= 0.
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\ea
$$

These two equations hold for every $\vecf{x} \in \mathcal{X}$,
so $\vecf{u} + \vecf{w}$ and $c\,\vecf{u}$ are in $\mathcal{X}^\perp$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-orthogonal-complement-subspace}
#### The complement of a single vector is a line

The one-element set $\mathcal{X} = \cb{(1, 2)}$ in $\reals^2$ is not a subspace:
$2\,(1, 2) = (2, 4)$ is not in it.
Its orthogonal complement is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{X}^\perp
&= \cb{\vecf{u} \in \reals^2 : u_1 + 2 u_2 = 0} \\
&= \cb{c\,(-2, 1) : c \in \reals},
\end{aligned}
$$

since $u_1 + 2u_2 = 0$ means

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vecf{u} &= (-2u_2, u_2) \\
&= u_2\,(-2, 1).
\end{aligned}
$$

That set is $\operatorname{span}\cb{(-2, 1)}$,
a subspace by @thm-span-subspace,
as @thm-orthogonal-complement-subspace says it must be.
It contains $(-2, 1)$, the vector @rem-orthogonal-perpendicular found perpendicular to $(1, 2)$.

:::
